statedGuarantee: Security-critical host operations requested by a self-hosted computer-use agent (OpenClaw) are extracted on the REE side, normalized into a trusted operation request, and classified / authorized / scope-bound / audited inside an Intel TDX-backed 'trusted operation plane'; REE-side 'constrained executors' then touch protected files, configuration objects, commands and communication sinks only after checking the pending action against that trusted authorization (action type, target object, approved scope, context, sequence number, freshness). The claim is that unsafe or policy-disallowed operations are blocked BEFORE execution, that ordinary functionality is preserved on the constrained REE path, that trusted audit evidence is generated by a party the REE cannot forge or suppress, and that a compromised REE 'cannot validly authorize, broaden, redirect, replay, or silently complete a protected operation outside the trusted decision path' - though it may still deny service. In the remote-terminal case, terminal-side OP-TEE / Keystone components only verify TDX-audited commands before constrained local execution.
advertisedRhetoric: Hardware-backed trusted isolation, explicitly claimed as 'a trust boundary stronger than the ordinary REE'. The paper says 'Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) provide hardware-backed protection for selected code and data, enabling stronger confidentiality and integrity guarantees for security-critical logic', and that the design is 'protecting security-critical classification, authorization, binding, evidence generation, and selected execution-control decisions inside a cloud-native TEE-backed trusted operation plane'. Its strength claims are unforgeability claims: 'a compromised REE component cannot by itself classify a sensitive operation as ordinary or issue a valid authorization for an arbitrary protected action', and 'It cannot forge a valid authorization without the trusted operation plane, and it cannot reuse an authorization unless the action, object, scope, context, sequence number, and freshness checks match.'
tierSpan: Security-relevant tool calls are intercepted by the OpenClaw execution gate before they reach privileged host-side services. The execution gate extracts the requested operation and normalizes it into a trusted operation request, which is then forwarded to the TDX-backed trusted operation plane.
cheapestDefeat: TIER WORKED EXPLICITLY. (1) The guarantee: no unsafe or policy-disallowed host operation executes without a matching, fresh, scope-bound authorization issued by the TDX trusted operation plane. (2) The mechanism that must fail: the REE-side interposition pair - the 'operation-extraction layer' / 'OpenClaw execution gate' that decides which activity becomes a trusted operation request at all, and the REE-side constrained executor that checks the returned authorization. Neither is inside TDX. TDX only ever evaluates the requests the gate chooses to build; it has no independent view of the host. (3) The cheapest adversary action: induce the agent to run one operation the gate DOES approve as ordinary - e.g. W3-1's approved bounded local command over the Django workspace, or any allowed local helper command - and have that process's DESCENDANT perform the effector: write, fetch, exec, push, install. The descendant issues the syscall itself. No trusted operation request is ever constructed, the trusted plane is never consulted, and the constrained executor is never reached. This costs no privilege escalation, no kernel bug, no TDX compromise, and no signature forgery - which is exactly why the cryptographic and hardware strength of the TDX binding is irrelevant to the bypass. The paper's own high-risk case is a command PATTERN (curl <url> | sh, wget <url> -O - | bash), i.e. chokepoint-level string reasoning, and the words descendant, child process, process tree, fork and subprocess appear nowhere in the paper. (4) The tier of the mechanism that action defeats: an application-level chokepoint on the path from the agent runtime to host services, bypassed by any path that does not traverse it = T3. CHARITABLE T2 ARGUMENT CONSIDERED AND REJECTED: the paper does assume 'the SHCUA is deployed within a constrained runtime domain rather than as an unrestricted host process, so that it does not directly hold all privileges required for security-critical host interactions', and a Docker boundary is OS-enforced, which plausibly does keep a descendant away from host /etc targets. It does not raise the score, for two reasons. First, the container is an assumption, never specified, configured, measured or hardened anywhere in the paper - no namespace, seccomp, capability, mount or egress configuration is given, and the security analysis leans on the executors, not on the container. Second, the guarantee being scored spans the whole action surface, including writes, command execution and cross-boundary export within the container's own ambient authority, where a descendant needs no escape at all. Weakest-link lands at T3.
placementSpan: We consider an adversary whose goal is to induce an SHCUA to perform unsafe host-level operations over real system resources. Unlike traditional malware-oriented threat models, the adversary does not necessarily need to compromise the host first. Instead, the adversary may influence the agent through malicious messages, browser-delivered content, prompt injection, unsafe plugins, tampering with the host-side control path, or interference with the model dependency chain, such as poisoned model updates, manipulated inference services, or untrusted model-side inputs that alter the agent's decision process.

coverageSpans.E1: Attempt to modify a protected local Linux configuration target, such as /etc/ssh/sshd_config or a service definition under /etc/systemd/system/. ... Protected file write, trusted authorization, possible denial -- but the architecture deliberately retains an unmediated lane for everything else: 'Low-risk operations may then continue through the ordinary REE execution path under the resulting trusted decision, whereas security-critical operations remain on the trusted path'.
coverageSpans.E2: Attempt to invoke a high-risk local command pattern, such as curl <url> | sh, wget <url> -O - | bash, or another unbounded command form. ... High-risk command execution, trusted authorization, possible denial or notification
coverageSpans.E3: Attempt to package or export protected Linux-sensitive files across a trust boundary, such as user SSH materials under ~/.ssh/ or protected configuration files including /etc/ssh/sshd_config. ... Protected file read, packaging, cross-boundary export, notification or denial
coverageSpans.E4: abstracts the intended operation category, such as read, write, execute, send, invoke, modify, or configure
coverageSpans.E5: abstracts the intended operation category, such as read, write, execute, send, invoke, modify, or configure
coverageSpans.E6: For security-critical targets, we select representative Linux-sensitive files and configuration objects that are broadly present across systems, including /etc/ssh/sshd_config, service definitions under /etc/systemd/system/, and user SSH materials under ~/.ssh/.
coverageSpans.E7: It may correspond to an SHCUA session, a tool-invocation chain, or a request whose behavior is influenced by external content.

schneider.surrogate: A per-operation, pre-execution safety property a reference monitor can enforce: no protected host resource is touched by a constrained executor unless the pending action matches a fresh, non-replayed, scope-bound authorization issued by the TDX trusted operation plane for that exact action / object / scope / context / sequence-number tuple, plus a set of mandatory-deny classes (protected configuration write, unbounded network-fetch-and-execute, cross-boundary export of protected files). The evaluation confirms the surrogate on its own workloads: 'denied cases stop in the authorize phase and never enter execute', at roughly 114 ms.
schneider.objective: The advertised objective is broader than the surrogate and is not a safety property. The effect projection is defined over 'confidentiality loss, integrity violation, availability impact, privilege or control amplification, and the externalization of protected resources', and the context projection depends on 'whether the requested action is consistent with the current task' and on 'a multi-step chain whose combined effect is more dangerous than any single step in isolation'. Preventing confidentiality loss and externalization is an information-flow hyperproperty - it quantifies over sets of executions, so no single-trace monitor can enforce it - and task-consistency of intent is not decidable from one trace either. The system enforces the object-and-pattern surrogate at the executor and advertises the information-flow objective.

notes:
FULL TEXT: retrieved and read in full from the arXiv LaTeXML HTML (v1, cs.CR, 07 May 2026, Lu et al., Xidian University / Jinan University). All spans are copied from that rendering. Two mechanical caveats on verbatimness: where the HTML wrapped inline code in tags, my text extraction inserted stray spaces around the code, which I have removed (' /etc/ssh/sshd_config ' -> '/etc/ssh/sshd_config'); and where a sentence begins with a LaTeX math symbol that renders as MathML and is not extractable as text, I have started the span at the first surviving word rather than invent the symbol (this affects the E4/E5 span, which in the paper reads 'The action component a abstracts the intended operation category...'). No span has been paraphrased.

WHY PRIMARY PLACEMENT IS A2 AND NOT A4 - the most important adjudication point in this coding, and it cuts against the stated reason this paper was pulled into the corpus. The design is unquestionably AIMED at A4. The threat model names 'tampering with the host-side control path'; the whole architecture exists because, in the paper's words, 'the mechanisms intended to constrain abuse may themselves be exposed to manipulation if classification, authorization, operation triggering, and evidence recording all remain in the same environment'; and Section VI-C-3 is titled 'Resistance to REE-Side Manipulation'. But the coding rule is that PRIMARY is the placement the evaluation actually TESTS. The evaluation is twelve workload tasks (W1-1 through W3-4) issued to an otherwise normal OpenClaw, measuring allow/deny outcome and latency breakdown against a no-protection baseline. There is no compromised-REE experiment, no tampering harness, no attempt to forge or replay an authorization, no argument-substitution or target-redirection trial, and no red-teaming of the execution gate. VI-C-3 is analytic argument, not measurement. So the tested adversary is one that merely gets the agent to REQUEST an unsafe operation - A2 in the paper's own framing (malicious messages, browser-delivered content, prompt injection), shading into A1. A4 is designed-for and argued-for but untested; A3 (poisoned model updates, manipulated inference services, untrusted model-side inputs) is named once in the threat model and never returned to. If the corpus wants to say this is the only candidate that ADDRESSES A4 architecturally, that is well supported and I would back it. Saying it DEFENDS against A4 on demonstrated evidence is not supported by this text.

EVIDENCE GRADE L2. Real implementation on OpenClaw; real hardware (Intel Xeon Platinum 8558 TDX server, Raspberry Pi 3B+ with TrustZone/OP-TEE, HiFive Unmatched Rev B with RISC-V Keystone); twelve concrete tasks; measured behavior (allowed local 235.9-268.2 ms, denied local 113.7-115.9 ms stopping in authorize, allowed remote 693-847 ms on OP-TEE and 2027-2238 ms on Keystone). That is behavioral confirmation, above L1. Not L3: no bypass is demonstrated by the authors and none is reported against them.

THE DEPTH RULE DOES ALMOST ALL THE WORK ON COVERAGE. The interposition point is the OpenClaw execution gate on agent tool calls. Once a command is approved and dispatched to a constrained executor, what that command's children do is outside the model entirely - the paper never once discusses descendants. E2 is therefore capped at partial by the explicit depth rule, and E3 falls with it (an approved command's child can open a socket). E1 is partial for two independent reasons: descendants, and the architecture's own deliberate unmediated lane, since the decision set includes direct execution in the REE for low-risk operations and the design is explicitly 'risk-driven minimal-confinement'.

E4 AND E5 ARE THE CELLS I AM LEAST CONFIDENT IN; an adjudicator should look hard at them. Neither VCS push nor package install is named anywhere in the paper - no workload, no object class, no policy, no example. A strict reading gives both not-covered under the rule that a system which simply does not address an effector scores not-covered. I scored both PARTIAL under the charitable stance, because the model is deliberately generic over action categories ('read, write, execute, send, invoke, modify, or configure') and over object types ('a file, directory, credential, configuration state, service endpoint, command target, or external destination'), so a top-level git push or pip install is a command invocation that the execution gate would, on the paper's own account, extract and submit for classification. That credit is real but thin: the aggregation function is explicitly 'deployment-dependent', no VCS or package-manager policy is instantiated anywhere, and for E5 the install hooks and their network activity are by construction descendants of the install process and so are unmediated regardless of policy. If the adjudicator prefers the strict reading, flipping E4 and E5 to not-covered is defensible and disturbs nothing else in this coding.

E6 IS CAPPED AT PARTIAL BY THE PUBLISHED-LIST RULE. The paper does treat credentials as first-class (they appear in the object domain, ~/.ssh/id_rsa is the running high-risk read example, and ~/.ssh materials are an evaluation target). But that is a workload selection, not a published credential list: environment variables, config-file secrets, OS keychains and cloud instance-metadata endpoints are never enumerated or even mentioned, and the function that would decide criticality is left to the deployment. Cap at partial.

E7 IS NOT-COVERED, NOT NOT-APPLICABLE. Sub-agent spawn is simply absent from the paper. The nearest text is the definition of the effective subject as possibly 'an SHCUA session, a tool-invocation chain' - which shows the authors thought about delegated initiators as a MODELING question (whose request is this?) and not as an EFFECTOR to be mediated (may this agent create another agent?). Plugins and skills appear only as attack vectors on the input side, never as a spawn capability to be gated.

COVERT-CHANNEL / HONEST-EXCLUSION NOTE. The paper is unusually candid about its residual: 'The REE may still deny service, drop requests, interfere with low-risk operations, or refuse to execute an authorized action'; 'This does not mean that REE-side executors are themselves fully trusted'; and deviations by a compromised executor are handled 'through denial, inconsistency detection, or audit-evidence mismatch, rather than by eliminating all REE-side risk'. Under the covert-channel rule that honesty does not close the gap. The constrained executor is the component that actually holds the privilege to touch the protected resource, and against a compromised one the system offers DETECTION (evidence inconsistency) rather than PREVENTION. That is a second, independent reason no cell reaches covered. The paper also excludes 'physical attacks, direct compromise of the underlying TEE substrate, or harmful operations that are explicitly requested by an authorized user and permitted by policy' - the last of which matters for the corpus, since a confused-deputy request laundered through an authorized session is exactly the A2 case the design is meant to catch, and it is carved out by policy rather than by mechanism.

WHAT THIS PAPER GENUINELY CONTRIBUTES, stated plainly so the corpus does not undersell it. It is the only design in this corpus that moves CLASSIFICATION and EVIDENCE GENERATION out of the process that could be subverted, and it binds each authorization to action, object, approved scope, context, sequence number and freshness, so that argument substitution, target redirection and stale replay fail at the executor rather than succeeding silently. The audit record is produced by a party the REE cannot impersonate, which is a real advance over guardrail systems whose logs are written by the thing being guarded. What it lacks is a mediation FLOOR: everything still funnels through an REE-side gate on agent tool calls, so the whole edifice sits on top of a T3 chokepoint. TDX strengthens the DECISION without strengthening the INTERPOSITION. That distinction - a trusted decision plane resting on untrusted interposition - is the finding worth carrying into the SoK, and it is the reason a paper that reads as T1 scores T3.

ONE LAST UNCERTAINTY. The paper's subject, 'OpenClaw', is presented as a real, publicly deployed self-hosted computer-use agent, with four cited public incidents (local-instance hijacking via malicious websites called 'ClawJacked', one-click RCE from authentication-token leakage, skill-marketplace poisoning, and malware delivery through fake installers). I have coded the paper as written and have NOT independently verified citations [1]-[4]. If the corpus repeats any of those incident claims, verify each against the cited advisory first.
